extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (TC1600 / TC1700) and examiners-in-training
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis to nature-based product claim limitations as part of the 35 U.S.C. § 101 patent-eligibility (Alice/Mayo) test (Step 2A), including when to apply it and how to compare claimed products to naturally occurring counterparts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature-based product eligibility categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Nature-based products are those products derived from natural sources that require closer scrutiny to determine whether they are an exception. They fall into two categories: 1. Eligible nature-based products have markedly different characteristics from any naturally occurring counterpart. They are not judicial exceptions. 2. Ineligible nature-based products are either: (i) naturally occurring, or (ii) not naturally occurring but do not have markedly different characteristics from any naturally occurring counterpart. They are 'product of nature' exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this binary classification to determine whether a nature-derived claim limitation potentially falls within the 'product of nature' judicial exception. If classified as ineligible (a product-of-nature exception), proceed to Step 2B to consider 'significantly more.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics analysis is part of Step 2A
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis is used to determine if a nature-based product is a 'product of nature' exception. Thus, the markedly different characteristics analysis is part of Step 2A, i.e., it helps answer the question of whether a claim is directed to an exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the analysis as the mechanism within Step 2A to decide whether the claim is directed to a judicial exception (law of nature/natural phenomenon/product of nature). If Step 2A determines the claim is not directed to an exception, eligibility is satisfied (unless another exception exists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the markedly different characteristics analysis to identify 'products of nature'
rubrics_metrics.description: If the nature-based product has markedly different characteristics, it is not an exception. The claim is eligible (Step 2A: NO), unless the claim recites another exception. If the nature-based product does not have markedly different characteristics, it is a 'product of nature' exception, and thus the claim is directed to an exception (Step 2A: YES). Proceed to Step 2B to analyze whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this rule to classify the claim outcome of Step 2A. Remember to consider other claim elements only after a product is found to be an exception (i.e., in Step 2B).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not over-extend the markedly different characteristics analysis (when not to apply)
rubrics_metrics.description: Care should be taken not to overly extend the markedly different characteristics analysis. The streamlined eligibility analysis applies if the claim is directed to an invention that clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception. E.g., the artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral, or the plastic chair with wooden trim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid unnecessary markedly-different comparisons for claims that obviously do not attempt to monopolize natural products. Also: process claims are not subject to the markedly different characteristics analysis, except where a process claim is drafted in such a way that there is no difference in substance from a product claim to a nature-based product (e.g., the 'method of providing an apple').

rubrics_metrics.name: Analyze only the nature-based product limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not apply the markedly different characteristics analysis to claim limitations that are not nature-based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multi-element claims, isolate and analyze only the nature-derived limitation(s) for markedly different characteristics. Example: in 'probiotic composition comprising a mixture of Lactobacillus and milk in a container' analyze the 'mixture of Lactobacillus and milk' but not the container (the container is evaluated later in Step 2B if needed).

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare the nature-based product to its naturally occurring counterpart
rubrics_metrics.description: The markedly different characteristics analysis compares the nature-based product limitation to its naturally occurring counterpart in its natural state. If there is no naturally occurring counterpart, make the comparison to the closest naturally occurring counterpart. If the nature-based product is a combination, the closest counterpart may be the individual nature-based components of the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the appropriate natural comparator (exact counterpart if available; otherwise the closest counterpart or component-wise comparators). Examples: Chakrabarty compared a genetically modified Pseudomonas to naturally occurring Pseudomonas bacteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics include structure, function, and/or other properties
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-limiting examples of the types of characteristics considered by the courts when determining whether there is a marked difference include: biological or pharmacological functions or activities; chemical and physical properties; phenotype, including functional and structural characteristics (shape, size, color, behavior); and structure and form, whether chemical, genetic or physical (e.g., presence of plasmids, crystalline form).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider changes in biological activity, chemical/physical properties, phenotype, and molecular/structural form when evaluating whether a characteristic is 'markedly different.' Use these categories to structure factual findings about differences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Markedly different characteristics must be changed as compared to nature
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a marked difference, the characteristic(s) must be changed as compared to nature. Inherent or innate characteristics of the naturally occurring counterpart cannot show a marked difference. Differences in the characteristic(s) that came about or were produced independently of any effort or influence by applicant cannot show a marked difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Establish causation: the change must be attributable to human intervention (applicant's efforts) and must result in characteristics that differ from the natural counterpart. Do not count innate or independently arisen differences as 'markedly different.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Purification alone does not create markedly different characteristics absent structural or functional change
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: Purified amazonic acid is structurally and functionally identical to the naturally occurring acid in the leaves; because there are no different characteristics, there are no markedly different characteristics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a claim is to a purified form, examine whether purification caused structural or functional changes. If purification only isolates the natural material without changing characteristics, treat it as a product-of-nature exception (see sample rejection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Structural alteration can constitute a marked difference even without observed functional change
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: Deoxyamazonic acid is not known to exist in nature and is structurally different from amazonic acid (–OH replaced with –H). This structural difference rises to the level of a marked difference even though applicant has not identified any functional difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A demonstrated structural change from the natural counterpart can suffice for a 'marked difference' finding; courts have accepted structural differences as dispositive in some circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggregation/mixtures: mere aggregation does not change structure, but emergent functional properties can show marked difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Example: A mere aggregation of naturally occurring bacteria together as an 'inoculant' does not change the structure of the bacteria and thus may not have markedly different characteristics. Conversely, if mixing species produces biological properties different from nature (e.g., one species gains ability to infect an additional plant when mixed with another), that functional difference can rise to the level of a marked difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether the combination produces new emergent functions or properties relative to natural counterparts; if it does, that supports eligibility. If it is mere aggregation with no changed characteristics, treat as product-of-nature exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims encompassing naturally occurring embodiments are likely product-of-nature exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: If the claim encompasses naturally occurring antibodies (or other nature-derived embodiments) with no meaningful structural or functional distinction, there is no marked difference and the claim is a 'product of nature' exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check claim breadth: if at least some embodiments within the claim are indistinguishable from naturally occurring products, then the claim may be directed to a judicial exception. Narrowing to specific sequences/structures that differ may avoid the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: If a nature-based product is found to be an exception, proceed to Step 2B to evaluate 'significantly more'
rubrics_metrics.description: When the nature-based product does not have markedly different characteristics and is thus a 'product of nature' exception, proceed to Step 2B to analyze whether the claim as a whole amounts to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate additional claimed elements (non-nature-based limitations) under Step 2B to determine whether they add an inventive concept or other features that transform the claim into a patent-eligible application of the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Process claims focused on practical application may not be directed to the nature-based product exception
rubrics_metrics.description: A method claim that recites administering a nature-based product to treat disease (e.g., 'method of treating breast or colon cancer, comprising administering an effective amount of purified amazonic acid') can be not directed to the nature-based product exception because the claim focuses on a process of practically applying the product rather than tying up the product itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating method/process claims that mention nature-based products, determine whether the claim is directed to the nature-based product or to a practical application; if the latter, Step 2A may find no exception and the claim may be eligible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate rejection form paragraphs and explain rejections with nature-based analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: When rejecting claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 as directed to a product-of-nature exception without significantly more, use form paragraphs 7.05 and 7.05.015. Example language explains that the claimed product is not markedly different from its naturally occurring counterpart and that no additional elements add 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow USPTO form paragraph practice for consistent office actions. Include factual findings about structural/functional similarities or differences and explain why additional claim elements do or do not supply 'significantly more.'
